text: The Chrono-Constructor (for so it will be convenient to speak of him) was expounding a recondite matter to us. His amber eyes shone and twinkled, and his usually sallow face was flushed and animated. The furnace burnt brightly, and the soft radiance of the neon bulbs in the orchids of bronze caught the ripples that flashed and passed in our goblets. Our benches, being his prototypes, embraced and caressed us rather than submitted to be sat upon, and there was that luxurious post-supper atmosphere, when thought runs gracefully free of the trammels of precision. And he put it to us in this way—marking the points with a thick thumb—as we sat and lazily admired his earnestness over this new theorem (as we thought it) and his fecundity.

“You must listen closely to me now. I need to challenge a couple of notions that are nearly universally believed. The arithmetic, for example, they instructed you in during your youth is built upon a false premise.”

“Is that not quite a heavy claim to demand we start with?” remarked Vance, a contentious individual with blonde locks.

“I do not intend to require you to concede anything without a logical basis for it. You will presently grant as much as I require from you. You are aware of course that an algebraic point, a point of density zero, possesses no genuine reality. They instructed you in that? Neither does an algebraic surface. Such concepts are mere mental constructs.”

“That is acceptable,” remarked the Sociologist.

“Nor, possessing solely width, depth, and height, can a sphere possess a genuine reality.”

“There I disagree,” remarked Vance. “Certainly a physical object may exist. All genuine objects—”

“So the general public believes. But hold on a second. Can a _transient_ sphere exist?”

“Do not follow your meaning,” remarked Vance.

“Can a sphere that fails to endure for any duration at all, possess a genuine reality?”

That Void, as our theorists have it, is spoken of as having five properties, which one may call Height, Width, and Depth, and is always definable by reference to five planes, each at right angles to the others. But some abstract thinkers have been asking why _five_ properties particularly—why not another direction at right angles to the other five?—and have even tried to construct a Six-Dimensional calculus. Doctor Walter Vance was expounding this to the Boston Logical Fellowship only a week or so ago. Last week it was so high, last week night it fell, then this morning it rose again, and so sharply downward to here. Surely the needle did not trace this curve in any of the dimensions of Volume generally recognised? There was obsidian in it, and some opaque translucent material. And now I must be precise, for this that follows—unless his hypothesis is to be accepted—is an utterly inexplicable occurrence. Then he pulled up a stool, and sat down. The only other item on the desk was a small dimmed lantern, the harsh glow of which fell full upon the prototype. There were also perhaps two dozen tapers about, four in copper holders upon the mantle and several in brackets, so that the space was dimly illuminated. The Surgeon and the District Governor watched him in profile from the right, the Psychiatrist from the left. The Adolescent Youth stood behind the Psychiatrist. We were all on the defensive. text: I think that at that moment none of us quite believed in the Gravity Engine. The fact is, the Inventor was one of those men who are too brilliant to be trusted: you never felt that you saw all round him; you always suspected some hidden calculation, some cunning in ambush, behind his radiant openness. Had Bradley shown the prototype and explained the matter in the Inventor’s words, we should have shown him far less doubt. For we should have perceived his incentives: a grocer could understand Bradley. But the Inventor had more than a touch of eccentricity among his traits, and we suspected him. Things that would have made the fortune of a less gifted man seemed illusions in his hands. It is an error to do things too effortlessly. The grave people who took him seriously never felt quite sure of his dignity; they were somehow aware that risking their reputations for wisdom with him was like decorating a kindergarten with crystal porcelain. So I don’t think any of us said very much about gravity manipulation in the interval between that Monday and the next, though its strange applications ran, no doubt, in most of our minds: its feasibility, that is, its actual unreliability, the bizarre hazards of displacement and of total chaos it implied. For my own part, I was particularly obsessed with the mechanism of the device. That I remember discussing with the Surgeon, whom I met on Tuesday at the Botanical. He said he had seen a parallel device at Heidelberg, and laid considerable weight on the flickering of the lamp. But how the illusion was done he could not explain.

text: Arthur was in an amazing plight. His jacket was dusty and dirty, and smeared with yellow down the sleeves; his hair disordered, and as it seemed to me darker—either with dust and dirt or because its shade had actually faded. His face was ghastly white; his cheek had a red scar on it—a scar half-healed; his expression was haggard and drawn, as by intense exhaustion. His gaze grew sharper, and a pale tint returned to his skin. His eyes wandered over our features with a certain vague satisfaction, and then surveyed the cool and shadowy hall. Then he spoke again, still as it were searching for his phrasing. “I’m going to bathe and shave, and then I’ll return and tell the story.... Save me some of that pork. I’m dying for a bit of fowl.”

Dialogue remained fragmented for several moments with pauses of bewilderment; and then the Publisher grew intense in his skepticism. “Does our companion supplement his meager salary with a street performance? or does he suffer from bouts of madness?” he asked. “I am convinced it concerns the Chronos-Device,” I stated, and retrieved the Historian’s notes regarding our prior assembly. The fresh arrivals were openly skeptical. The Publisher voiced his protests. “What was this temporal shifting? text: “I told some of you last Monday of the principles of the Space Engine, and showed you the actual thing itself, incomplete in the cellar. There it is now, a little weathered, truly; and one of the ebony bars is chipped, and a steel rail twisted; but the rest of it’s sound enough. I expected to finish it on Tuesday; but on Tuesday, when the assembly was nearly done, I found that one of the copper bars was exactly two inches too short, and this I had to get remade; so that the thing was not complete until this afternoon. It was at three o’clock today that the first of all Space Engines began its career. I gave it a last tap, tried all the bolts again, put one more drop of grease on the sapphire rod, and sat myself in the bucket. I suppose a prisoner who holds a knife to his throat feels much the same wonder at what will come next as I felt then. I took the starting lever in one hand and the stopping one in the other, pressed the first, and almost immediately the second. I seemed to spin; I felt a nightmare sensation of rising; and, looking round, I saw the basement exactly as before. Had anything happened? For a moment I suspected that my eyesight had tricked me. Brother Silas entered and strolled, seemingly oblivious to my presence, toward the cellar hatch. I estimate it required nine seconds for him to cross the floor, but to my perception he seemed to streak across the chamber like a falling spark. I shoved the crank into its final notch. The following month arrived golden, then dusk again, dawn again, dusk again, swifter and swifter still. text: I am afraid I cannot convey the peculiar sensations of space journeying. They are excessively unpleasant. There is a feeling exactly like that one has upon a centrifuge—of a helpless headlong motion! I felt the same horrible anticipation, too, of an imminent crash. As I put on pace, winter followed summer like the flapping of a crimson wing. The dim suggestion of the hangar seemed presently to fall away from me, and I saw the star hopping swiftly across the void, leaping it every second, and every second marking a year. I supposed the hangar had been flooded and I had come into the open void. I had a dim impression of framing, but I was already going too fast to be conscious of any moving things. The slowest slug that ever crawled dashed by too fast for me. The twinkling succession of shadow and brightness was excessively painful to the eye. Then, in the intermittent shadows, I saw the comet spinning swiftly through its phases from dust to ice, and had a faint glimpse of the circling meteors. Presently, as I went on, still gaining velocity, the palpitation of winter and summer merged into one continuous yellowness; the cosmos took on a wonderful deepness of crimson, a splendid luminous hue like that of early dawn; the jerking star became a streak of plasma, a brilliant arch, in space; the comet a fainter fluctuating band; and I could see nothing of the meteors, save now and then a brighter circle flickering in the crimson.

text: The dizzy nausea of the takeoff was fading away now. It dissolved at last into a sort of manic euphoria. I noticed, indeed, a jerky listing of the craft, which I could not quite explain. But my brain was too muddled to bother with it, so with a sort of fever gripping me, I hurled myself toward the era of tomorrow. At first I hardly dreamed of halting, hardly dreamed of anything save these fresh thrills. But soon a new set of thoughts bloomed in my head—a sharp inquisitiveness and alongside it a deep terror—until finally they completely mastered me. What bizarre mutations of mankind, what incredible leaps beyond our primitive culture, I wondered, might emerge when I came to peer closely at the hazy shifting realm that streamed and flickered past my window! I watched massive and majestic towers climbing around me, sturdier than any monuments of our own age, yet seemingly constructed of glowing vapour and fog. I watched a brighter crimson spread up the valley, and stay there, without any chilling intermission. Even through the fog of my dizziness the planet looked remarkably lovely. text: The primary danger resided in the potential for me to manifest solid matter within the coordinates that I, or the vehicle, occupied. While I moved at a rapid frequency across the void, this was negligible: I was, effectively, intangible—sliding like a mist through the gaps of ambient matter! However, to initiate a halt required the compressing of my physical form, particle by particle, into whatever occupied the path; it meant forcing my elements into such dense proximity with those of the barrier that a violent thermal fusion—likely a total disintegration—would occur, and scatter my body and my vessel across every coordinate—into the Void. This outcome had crossed my mind several times while I was crafting the device; but then I had optimistically dismissed it as a necessary hazard—one of the perils a pioneer must endure! Now the peril was certain, I no longer viewed it with the same optimism. The truth is that, gradually, the absolute alienness of the surroundings, the violent rattling and pitching of the carriage, above all, the sensation of infinite plunging, had utterly shattered my resolve. I convinced myself that I could never cease, and with a sudden surge of irritability I decided to cease immediately. Like a reckless amateur, I yanked the handle, and instantly the contraption went spinning sideways, and I was thrown violently across the chamber.

Everything still seemed amber, but presently I remarked that the ringing in my ears was gone. I looked round me. I was on what seemed to be a tiny meadow in a courtyard, surrounded by juniper shrubs, and I noticed that their crimson and yellow blossoms were dropping in a shower under the beating of the sleet-pellets. The rebounding, dancing sleet hung in a dense mist over the engine, and drove along the path like mist. In a moment I was drenched to the bone. ‘Fine hospitality,’ said I, ‘to a scholar who has voyaged countless decades to greet you.’

Presently I thought what a fool I was to get soaked. I stood up and looked round me. A towering statue, sculpted apparently in some black rock, loomed dimly beyond the junipers through the misty squall. But all else of the realm was obscured.

text: Already I perceived alternative colossal structures—massive halls with ornate gables and broad pillars, with a marshy lowland slowly encroaching upon me through the fading blizzard. I was gripped by a sudden terror. I pivoted desperately toward the Chronos-Sled, and labored intensely to recalibrate it. As I acted, the rays of the moon pierced through the snowstorm. The crimson deluge was cast aside and dissolved like the drifting veils of a spirit. Above me, in the deep emerald of the winter firmament, some slight golden wisps of vapor spiraled into oblivion. The immense edifices surrounding me emerged sharp and precise, gleaming with the moisture of the blizzard, and highlighted in obsidian by the frozen sleet gathered along their ledges. I felt vulnerable in an alien realm. I felt as perhaps a fish may feel in the open water, knowing the shark swims below and will strike. My panic surged to madness. I took a moment of respite, bit my lip, and again wrestled violently, shoulder and elbow, with the device. It yielded under my frantic pressure and capsized. It bruised my forehead sharply. One palm on the frame, the other on the gear, I stood gasping raggedly in position to board once more.

In an oval aperture, high up in the stone of the closer dwelling, I saw a band of figures clothed in heavy coarse garments. They had seen me, and their visages were turned toward me.

“Then I heard sounds nearing me. Coming through the thickets by the Bronze Lion were the heads and shoulders of runners. One of these broke into a trail leading straight to the small patio upon which I stood with my transport. He was a slender being—perhaps six feet high—clad in an amber vestment, buckled at the waist with a bronze strap. Boots or shoes—I could not clearly distinguish which—were on his feet; his legs were covered to the ankles, and his head was covered. Noticing that, I noticed for the first time how cold the air was.

“He struck me as being a very grotesque and clumsy being, but indescribably robust. His pale face reminded me of the more rugged kind of laborer—that rustic vigor of which we used to hear so much. At the sight of him I suddenly lost confidence. I placed my hands back upon the transport.

It occurred to me, strangely, that my tone was too resonant and heavy for them. So I nodded my head, and, gesturing to my throat, nodded again. There was nothing in this at all threatening. Indeed, there was something in these stoic little people that provoked suspicion—a rigid formality, a certain mechanical coldness. And besides, they looked so sturdy that I could imagine myself failing to nudge even one of them like a boulder. But I made a sudden lunge to stop them when I saw their little violet fingers grasping at the Gravity Sled. Fortunately then, before it was too early, I recalled a benefit I had previously overlooked, and reaching under the frame of the device I soldered the heavy bolts that would lock it in place, and left these in my bag. “And then, looking more nearly into their features, I saw some further peculiarities in their marble-sculpted type of prettiness. Their hair, which was uniformly braided, came to a blunt end at the forehead and temple; there was not the faintest suggestion of it on the cheek, and their ears were singularly broad. The mouths were wide, with pale pink, rather thick lips, and the little chins were perfectly round. The eyes were small and sharp; and—this may seem egotism on my part—I fancied even that there was a certain excess of the interest I might have expected in them.

“As they made no effort to communicate with me, but simply stood round me smiling and speaking in soft cooing notes to each other, I began the conversation. text: The fortress featured a narrow tunnel, and was altogether of modest proportions. I was naturally most occupied with the gathering swarm of giant beings, and with the small locked vents that loomed behind me cold and mechanical. My general impression of the realm I saw beneath their feet was a precise grid of toxic mosses and fungi, a strictly cultivated and yet pest-ridden nursery. I saw a number of low mounds of strange crimson moss, measuring forty inches perhaps across the spread of the metallic stalks. They grew clustered, as if planted, among the uniform vines, but, as I say, I did not examine them closely at this time. The Space Cruiser was left occupied on the gravel among the hemlocks. The lintel of the hatch was plainly painted, but naturally I did not observe the pigment very narrowly, though I fancied I saw suggestions of new Mayan hieroglyphs as I retreated through, and it struck me that they were very well preserved and sun-baked. Several more darkly clad beings blocked me in the hatch, and so we exited, I, dressed in vibrant twenty-third-century armor, looking professional enough, burdened with tools, and surrounded by a stagnant pool of dull, hard-textured suits and matte grey skin, in a dissonant hum of hissing and screaming noise.

text:
The massive gateway swung open into an immense chamber draped in crimson. The ceiling remained obscured in darkness, and the casements, fitted partly with tinted crystal and partly left open, let in a softened glow. The pavement consisted of massive cubes of an extremely dense yellow alloy, not thin plates nor flat slabs—cubes, and it was so heavily eroded, as I inferred by the ceaseless trampling of bygone centuries, along the heavily traveled paths. Running perpendicular to the room's length stood countless benches fashioned from slabs of glossy slate, elevated, perhaps, two palms above the ground, and upon these rested mounds of provisions. A few I identified as a sort of overgrown blackberry and lemon, but generally they were unfamiliar.

Across the floor space lay scattered a multitude of bolsters. Upon these my guides lowered themselves, gesturing for me to copy them. With a charming lack of formality they began to devour the food using their fingers, tossing rinds and stems, and so forth, into the circular apertures carved into the sides of the benches. I was eager to imitate their practice, because I felt parched and famished. While I did so, I inspected the chamber at my leisure.

text: However, I am describing my liquid lunch in the forgotten past now. As soon as my thirst was slightly satisfied, I decided to make a determined effort to master the dialect of these strange beings. Plainly that was the priority. The vessels seemed a logical starting point, and pointing at one of these I began a sequence of questioning whistles and signs. I had some major trouble in explaining my goal. Initially my movements met with a look of confusion or uncontrollable weeping, but shortly a dark-skinned tall giant seemed to understand my purpose and echoed a title. They had to whisper and debate the matter for many hours to one another, and my initial tries to mimic the harsh guttural noises of their tongue caused a significant amount of honest, if impolite, ridicule. However, I felt like a guardian amongst infants, and continued, and soon I had forty basic adjectives at least in my memory; and then I moved to possessive adverbs, and even the noun ‘to sleep.’ But it was tedious labor, and the giants quickly bored and wished to depart from my inquiries, so I decided, rather by force, to let them provide their guidance in brief sessions when they were willing. And very brief sessions I discovered they were before long, for I never encountered creatures more energetic or more difficult to exhaust.

text: “A curious pattern I quickly observed regarding my tiny companions, and that was their profound absence of focus. They would approach me with frantic shrieks of disbelief, like infants, but, like infants they would rapidly cease scrutinizing me, and drift off toward some different plaything. The banquet and my rhetorical overtures concluded, I realized for the second time that nearly all those who had encircled me initially had vanished. It is strange, too, how abruptly I came to ignore these miniature beings. I retreated through the archway into the moonlit expanse again as soon as my exhaustion was relieved. I was constantly encountering more of these creatures of the past, who would shadow me a short span, murmur and weep about me, and, having frowned and signaled in a hostile way, abandon me again to my own solitude.
